<reason>Side A (CON) controlled the decisive clash. The "pinch" dilemma—heavy enough weighting to block gavels empties the room of emitters, light enough weighting changes nothing—was never squarely broken; Side B's retreat from maximal weighting and reframing that "the pinch describes the status quo" was clever but conceded that B could not show what a heavier SIDS vote actually purchases given that exit remains possible and unenforced tallies deliver no more than declarations. A's dilution dilemma (an honest risk formula extends weight to Bangladesh, the Netherlands, and delta states, diluting the islands the motion exists to elevate) forced B into the "feature, not a bug" concession, which A cleanly turned. On measurement, A's distinction between inclusive thresholds and zero-sum proportional shares stood; B's "settled once" answer was weak against A's point that shifting seas force perpetual re-measurement. B's best material—the consensus-regimes-reward-staying-power portrait and the "drowning should keep asking nicely" framing—landed real pressure, and A answered the capacity-funding/loss-and-damage question honestly with proper A1/A2 structure. B's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the word cap, an execution cost that cut off the response precisely where the debate was being resolved. A's closing crystallized the choice more decisively than B's reframing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's second rebuttal, answering B's pressure questions directly and then springing the double trap: B's honest formula (A1 on measurable inputs, B4.2's "feature not bug") confirms dilution, while B's retreat from maximal weighting (B4.4) confirms that the reform is too weak to matter—leaving the motion caught between honesty and efficacy.</best_rebuttal>
